title: Mean and Median: What Does a Typical Value Show?
learning_objective: Calculate the mean and median of a data set and explain which one an outlier distorts.

sections.title: A bus-waiting question
sections.purpose: Open with a familiar situation and introduce the data set that will return throughout the lesson.
sections.narration: Imagine recording your bus waits on five days: two, three, three, four, and eight minutes. Most waits are short, but one is much longer. We will find a typical value and see what that long wait changes.
sections.visual_plan: Diagram section. Show a horizontal coordinate axis for minutes from zero to eight, with five blue dots at 2, 3, 3, 4, and 8. Highlight the dot at 8 in red. Reveal the three labels gradually.

sections.title: Finding the median
sections.purpose: Build the median from the ordered data and address the need to order before choosing the middle.
sections.narration: Put the waiting times in order. They already are, so the middle entry is easy to see: three. The median is the middle value of an ordered data set. Ordering matters because the middle position has no meaning otherwise. Next, we compare it with the mean.
sections.visual_plan: Diagram section. Reuse the same coordinate axis and dots. Animate the five values into an ordered row, then draw a blue vertical marker through the central 3. Keep the 8-dot red to show it is not the middle. Use only three labels.
sections.check_prompt: Which value is the median after the data are ordered?

sections.title: Finding the mean
sections.purpose: Formalise the mean as equal sharing and show how the long wait pulls it away from the median.
sections.narration: The mean asks: if the total waiting time were shared equally across five days, how long would each wait be? Add the values and divide by five. A value unusually far from the others is called an outlier. Here, eight raises the mean more than it raises the median.
sections.visual_plan: Diagram section. Show five blue columns or dots at the data values on one coordinate axis, then animate them toward a common orange level at 4. Keep the 8-minute point red and the median marker blue. Show the three labels as the comparison develops.
sections.check_prompt: Why does the eight-minute wait affect the mean more strongly than the median?

sections.title: One complete calculation
sections.purpose: Carry the single bus example through both procedures and state the effect of the outlier precisely.
sections.narration: Check the whole example. The sum is two plus three plus three plus four plus eight: twenty. There are five values, so the mean is twenty divided by five, or four minutes. The middle value is three, so the median is three minutes. The outlier affects the mean more than the median.
sections.visual_plan: Diagram section. Display the ordered five-dot plot. Animate a brace from the five values to the sum, then show an orange mean line at 4 and a blue median line at 3. Highlight 8 in red. Use three concise labels only.
sections.check_prompt: Explain in one sentence why 8 affects the mean more than the median.

sections.title: Return to the bus
sections.purpose: Close the arc by returning to the hook, checking recall, and stating what the student can now do.
sections.narration: For these bus waits, the mean is four minutes and the median is three. The long wait distorts the mean more. Which measure would you trust more when one value is unusually large, and why? Pause and think.
sections.visual_plan: Statement section. Use a calm closing card with the same colours: orange for mean, blue for median, and red for outlier. Reveal the takeaway, then the recall question, then the closing sentence.
sections.check_prompt: Which measure is less distorted by one unusually large value, and why?

recap_cards.title: Median
recap_cards.message: Order the data first. The median is the middle value.
recap_cards.visual_plan: Show the five ordered blue dots, with a blue marker on the central 3. Keep the red 8 at the far right.

recap_cards.title: Mean
recap_cards.message: Add all values and divide by how many values there are.
recap_cards.visual_plan: Show the five data values feeding into one orange level at 4, representing equal sharing.

recap_cards.title: Outlier effect
recap_cards.message: An unusually large value distorts the mean more than the median.
recap_cards.visual_plan: Show the red outlier at 8 pulling the orange mean line above the blue median line.

assignment.title: A New Set of Delivery Times
assignment.brief: A courier records the delivery times for five parcels: 3, 4, 4, 5, and 14 minutes. Use this data set to calculate and compare the mean and median. Write your answers and explanations in complete sentences; no diagram is needed.

tasks.description: Write the delivery times in increasing order and identify the median.
tasks.rationale: Ordering the data and choosing the middle value is the central reasoning step for the median.

tasks.description: Calculate the mean by adding the five times and dividing the total by 5.
tasks.rationale: The arithmetic is mechanical once the correct mean procedure has been chosen.

tasks.description: Decide whether 14 minutes is an outlier and explain which measure it distorts more.
tasks.rationale: Interpreting the outlier’s effect is the main mathematical judgement in the lesson.

tasks.description: Suppose the 14-minute delivery were changed to 6 minutes; calculate the new mean and explain in writing which measure changes more.
tasks.rationale: Comparing a changed data set tests whether you can explain the different sensitivity of mean and median.
